Neil shared a cool story of how a skunkworks project turned Nvidia's gaming GPUs into AI chips, starting in 2015:

"I remember reading some of the lab notebooks of some of my managers when I was at Nvidia. 

They would visit these small ML conferences like ICML or NeurIPS at the time, and they would just take note of these papers. 

"What's really interesting is that these grad students are using gaming Nvidia GPUs in order to train their large models. We should double-click on this and figure out what's going on here."

By 2015, 2016, Jensen had the conviction to double down on, "hey, this usage of our chips is only gonna grow. Let's put the first version of tensor cores on the chip." 

We're talking about taking this gaming chip, which is designed for painting pixels on a screen, and adapting it to do matrix multiplies.

It was early, and we would be competing against the graphics teams, essentially. 

You don't ever want to invest in the wrong technology, because that's opportunity cost that you could have allocated to some other functionality. 

And so we fought tooth and nail and got just a tiny bit of die area, maybe five, ten percent."

Neil on why AI spending today is different from the dot-com bubble:

"A lot of the investment in networking equipment historically was speculative. 

We anticipated this future demand for users that never came.

What's interesting about token consumption is that it's no longer speculative. People buy tokens because they're immediately valuable to them. 

You don't hoard tokens. You use them immediately.

This is even different from what we had two years ago, where there was a supply crunch for Hopper generation chips in 2023, 2024. 

In that period it was all training oriented spend, and training is inherently speculative.

I do think inference spend monotonically increases. There's no speculation on inference spend."

Neil Movva (@neilmovva) started his career at Nvidia, working on GPUs and kernels, and has an unusually deep understanding of inference, from software to chips to power.

We spend a lot of time on each of those layers, how they connect, and where the important tradeoffs are.

What makes this conversation special is how detailed it is (like a 401-level class), yet Neil makes it remarkably clear and easy to follow.

Today he runs Sail Research, a company building infrastructure for agents to make tokens as cheap as possible.

We discuss:
- Latency versus throughput
- Why there are no bad chips, only bad pricing
- The end of kernel engineering
- Buying chips and power no one else wants
- New chip architectures
- Nvidia lore + his contrarian view of the company
- Open source and the frontier labs

I learned a ton. Enjoy!

The tokenized stock race may be won through distribution instead of issuance.

Several issuers can offer tokenized exposure to the same equities, making the ability to attract traders and liquidity more important than the wrapper itself.

Binance launched bStocks on June 11 and generated $1.8B of volume within 24 days. Volume rose sharply to $14.7B in July across Binance spot and BNB Chain. Nearly 300,000 people had traded bStocks by the end of the month.

Binance entered after the specialist issuers and still reached 28% of tokenized stock value among the three largest issuers by the end of July. Those firms remained ahead even as Binance closed much of the gap within weeks.

Launching early creates a head start. Keeping that lead may depend on attracting traders and building liquidity around the product.

here’s how to do this workflow with Hermes:

1: Open Hermes

Use the normal Hermes Desktop app.
Hermes already installs FFmpeg, so you do not need to install that yourself. 

2: Give Hermes this instruction

Copy and paste this bro:

“Create a reusable skill called “YouTube Clipper”.
When I send you a YouTube URL and a start and end timestamp:
Download the highest-quality available video and audio using yt-dlp.
If yt-dlp is not installed, install it for me.
Cut the video exactly between my timestamps using FFmpeg.
Keep the original resolution and use high-quality output.
Make the cut frame-accurate.
Save the finished clip as an MP4.
Transcribe the finished clip using Whisper/faster-whisper.
Save the transcript as a TXT file.
Give the transcript to a Researcher sub-agent.
Have the Researcher identify the best quotes, hooks, claims and interesting points.
Give those findings to a Writer sub-agent.
Have the Writer create a strong X post/caption for the clip.
Return to me:
Finished HD clip
Transcript
Best quotes
Suggested hook
Suggested X caption
Save this entire process as a reusable skill.
After setup, whenever I send a YouTube URL followed by timestamps, automatically run this workflow.”

Hermes can create persistent reusable skills itself, rather than you manually coding them. 

3: Approve the setup

Hermes may ask permission to:

> Install yt-dlp
> Install transcription dependencies
> Create the skill
> Run terminal commands

Click approve.

You shouldn’t need to write any code yourself.

4: Set up transcription

You can simply tell Hermes:

“Set up the easiest free local transcription option for this skill.”

Hermes supports local faster-whisper, which doesn’t require an API key. 

There is also an official Whisper skill specifically designed for podcast/video transcription. 

5: Test it brev

“Send Hermes something like:
https://t.co/YwYzhVdsef
Cut 16:43 to 18:17.”

Hermes should now:

> Download video  > Cut 16:43–18:17 > Create HD MP4 > Transcribe it > Researcher analyses it > Writer creates caption > Returns everything

Hermes supports sub-agents for exactly this kind of separate research/writing work to nail this workflow.

To collaborate successfully, you have to do three things:

First, put your honest thoughts on the table for everybody to look at. Everyone's thoughts are different, and you have to be willing to look at them openly.

Second, know the art of thoughtful disagreement. Ask yourself: how do you work through disagreements to get a better answer than you would have come up with individually?

Third, if the disagreements remain, you have to have protocols for getting past that. In our case, we have an "idea meritocracy" through believability-weighted decision-making.

When you have a system where the best ideas win out, the results are going to be so much better than if you just stuck with the ideas inside your own head.

#Collaboration #IdeaMeritocracy #Teamwork #RayDalio

tweets.text:
Are merchants losing money via x402?

x402 just had one of the most amazing weeks in a while
> # of txns hit 1M-1.5M/day for the first time since ever
> Volume is also up by ~2x compared to July & June

Considering the massive pace at which # of txns grow, average x402 txn size hit the lowest point of $0.023 - $0.031 per txn.

Now, every x402 txn must be validated & broadcasted to the blockchain which can be done using your own self-hosted infra or via third-party facilitator.

BUT.... Most opt for third-party facilitator. 

Most popular ones are Coinbase CDP on Base and PayAI on Solana. Both charge $0.001 per settlement with 1,000 and 10,000 free settlements per month, respectively.

So.... $0.001 = ~32% - 43% of the avg x402 txn size

(The cost is 32% - 43% of GMV!!!)

If a merchant is expecting to sell a service cheaply in millions of microtransactions, the merchant has to really think long and hard about the pricing.

One thing I don't quite grasp yet is x402 batching — it went live earlier in May.

Batching batches 1,000s of txns into 1 txn and settle for $0.001 per batch which would effectively eliminate 90-99% of the cost.

But most (if not all) of the x402 transactions are currently "exact" which is 1 txn = 1 settlement.

Why is batching not adopted when it can save money?

Does the client tooling not support batching?

Is it the counter-party risk or the accounting hassle people are worried about?
